source_refs.note: Book p. 241-242: 13.3.1 Notation of Derivative, equations (iv)-(vi), dy/dx = f'(x), Note box, notation table (Leibniz, Newton, Lagrange, Euler), alternative form (vii), f'(a) as gradient at x = a

blocks.text:
Several notations are used for derivatives. We have used the functional symbol \(f'(x)\) for the derivative of \(f\) at \(x\). For the function \(y = f(x)\),
\[y + \delta y = f(x + \delta x) \quad \text{...(iv)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What does (iv) say? When \(x\) changes by a small amount \(\delta x\) (read "delta x"), the value of \(y\) changes by an amount \(\delta y\). The new input is \(x + \delta x\), so the new output is \(f(x + \delta x)\), and this new output equals the old \(y\) plus its change \(\delta y\).
A small step the book leaves out: subtract \(y = f(x)\) from both sides of (iv) to get the change in \(y\) alone:
\[\delta y = f(x+\delta x) - f(x)\]
It is this equation that is divided by \(\delta x\) in the next line.

Dividing both the sides of (iv) by \(\delta x\), we get
\[\dfrac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}\]
\[\text{...(v)}\]
Taking limit of both the sides of (v) as \(\delta x \to 0\), we have
\[\lim_{\delta x \to 0}\dfrac{\delta y}{\delta x}\]
\[= \lim_{\delta x \to 0}\dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}\]
\[\text{...(vi)}\]

\(\lim\limits_{\delta x \to 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}\) is denoted by \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), so (vi) is written as
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f'(x)\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The symbol \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is used for the derivative of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) and here it is not a quotient of \(dy\) and \(dx\). \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is also denoted by \(y'\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read the symbols:
\(\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}\): "delta y by delta x", an ordinary fraction: change in \(y\) divided by change in \(x\) (the average rate of change).
\(\frac{dy}{dx}\): "dee y by dee x", the limit of that fraction (the instantaneous rate of change). It is one symbol. You cannot cancel the \(d\)'s, and \(dy\) alone has no meaning here.
\(\frac{d}{dx}\) on its own is an instruction: "differentiate with respect to \(x\)". For example \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2})\) means "the derivative of \(x^{2}\)".
Now we write, in a table the notations for derivative of \(y = f(x)\) used by different mathematicians:

blocks.caption: Notations for the derivative of y = f(x) used by different mathematicians

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints Newton's notation as \(f^{\bullet}(x)\) or \(y^{\bullet}\), with the dot raised beside the letter like a power. In Newton's notation the dot is written directly above the letter: \(\dot{f}(x)\) or \(\dot{y}\) (read "f dot", "y dot"). Newton used it mainly for rates of change with respect to time, so in Physics \(\dot{s}\) is a velocity.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
All four notations mean exactly the same thing: the derivative of \(y = f(x)\). In this book you will mostly see Leibniz's \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and Lagrange's \(f'(x)\) (read "f dash x" or "f prime x").
Leibniz's notation shows which variable we differentiate with respect to (\(dx\) at the bottom). Lagrange's prime is shorter. Euler's \(D\) is an operator: \(D\) acting on \(f\) means "differentiate \(f\)".
The derivative at a point x = a

If we replace \(x + \delta x\) by \(x\) and \(x\) by \(a\), then the expression \(f(x + \delta x) - f(x)\) becomes \(f(x) - f(a)\) and the change \(\delta x\) in the independent variable, in this case, is \(x - a\).
So, the expression \(\frac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}\) is written as
\[\dfrac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a} \quad \text{...(vii)}\]
Taking the limit of the expression (vii) when \(x \to a\), gives
\[\lim_{x \to a}\dfrac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a} = f'(a)\]
Here \(f'(a)\) is called the derivative or gradient of \(f\) at \(x = a\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is this the same definition? In the first form the fixed point is \(x\) and the moving point is \(x + \delta x\). In the second form the fixed point is \(a\) and the moving point is \(x\). In both, the top is "change in \(f\)" and the bottom is "change in the input"; the change in the input is \(\delta x\) in one and \(x - a\) in the other. "\(\delta x \to 0\)" and "\(x \to a\)" say the same thing: the moving point comes closer and closer to the fixed point.
Geometrically, \(\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\) is the slope of the secant through \((a, f(a))\) and \((x, f(x))\); its limit is the slope (gradient) of the tangent at \(x = a\), as in 13.1.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick example of the second form (ours, not from the book): the gradient of \(f(x) = x^{2}\) at \(x = 3\).
\[\dfrac{f(x)-f(3)}{x-3} = \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}\]
\[= \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3} = x + 3,\ (x \ne 3)\]
\[f'(3) = \lim_{x \to 3}(x+3) = 6\]
This agrees with \(f'(x) = 2x\) (Example 3(b)) at \(x = 3\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Use the first form \(\lim\limits_{\delta x \to 0}\frac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}\) when the question asks for \(f'(x)\) or \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) in general. The second form \(\lim\limits_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\) is handy when a fixed point \(x = a\) is given. Either form earns full marks if the working is correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(y + \delta y = f(x+\delta x)\), so \(\delta y = f(x+\delta x) - f(x)\).
2. \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim\limits_{\delta x \to 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = f'(x)\).
3. \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is one symbol, not a fraction; it is also written \(y'\).
4. Notations: Leibniz \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), \(\frac{df}{dx}\); Newton \(\dot{y}\); Lagrange \(f'(x)\); Euler \(Df(x)\).
5. \(f'(a) = \lim\limits_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\) is the derivative (gradient) of \(f\) at \(x = a\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Cancelling the \(d\)'s in \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) to get \(\frac{y}{x}\). The symbol is not a fraction.
2. Reading \(\delta x\) as \(\delta \times x\). It is a single quantity, a change in \(x\).
3. Confusing \(f'(x)\) with \(f'(a)\): \(f'(x)\) is a function of \(x\); \(f'(a)\) is one number, the gradient at one point.
4. Forgetting to write "\(\lim\)" in each line until the limit is actually taken.
